title: Eli Lilly Advances As Inflammatory Bowel Disease Drug Reinforces Long-Term Confidence
content:
Eli Lilly and Co. shares are trading higher on Tuesday as the company is reporting new data on its treatment for ulcerative colitis (UC).

Omvoh Shows Durable Disease Clearance

Disease clearance was evaluated among patients who achieved clinical remission with Omvoh at one year in the LUCENT-2 maintenance study and continued treatment in LUCENT-3, an open-label extension study.

Eli Lilly’s recent data from the LUCENT-3 clinical trial shows that over 63.5% of patients treated with Omvoh (mirikizumab-mrkz) maintained disease clearance after four years.

This is a significant milestone, as it marks the first time an interleukin-23p19 inhibitor has demonstrated such durable disease clearance in patients with UC.

Stringent Measures Reinforce Long-Term Efficacy

Even at the most stringent measure — requiring endoscopic normalization in addition to symptomatic and histologic remission — 61.3% of patients who achieved it at one year maintained it through four years.

The long-term safety profile in patients with moderately to severely active UC was consistent with the known safety profile of Omvoh, with no new safety signals observed.

Of patients who completed one year of blinded Omvoh maintenance therapy in LUCENT-2 and continued to LUCENT-3, 12% reported a serious adverse event, while 7% discontinued treatment due to an adverse event.

Expanding Label Across Inflammatory Bowel Diseases

In January 2025, the FDA approved Omvoh (mirikizumab-mrkz) for moderately to severely active Crohn's disease in adults.

Omvoh received U.S. approval for two types of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). In October 2023, it received approval as a first-in-class treatment for moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (UC) in adults.

In February, the U.S. drugmaker released promising long-term data regarding its treatment for Crohn's disease, reporting that more than 90% of patients maintained steroid-free remission for three years with Omvoh.

The latest data from Eli Lilly's Phase 3 VIVID-2 study revealed clinical remission of 92.4%, and Corticosteroid-free clinical remission of 91.2%.

title: 'Uber won': Why Instacart might not stand a chance
content:
Uber (UBER) and Maplebear (CART) (Instacart's parent company) both reported quarterly earnings on Wednesday.

BNP Paribas US large-cap internet equity analyst Nick Jones joins Yahoo Finance's Josh Lipton to discuss the key differences between the two companies and why he thinks Uber has much more room to run.

Video Transcript

00:00 Speaker A

What makes Uber different, Nick than the competition? What what's their competitive edge and advantage?

00:09 Nick

The competitive advantage is Uber one. Um you probably know more and more people who have the subscription and the platform, the kind of the flywheel we see here is you can combine mobility with delivery. So not only can you take a cab or a robotaxi service or a taxi service somewhere, you can also use it to order food uh at a hotel or to your home and you can increasingly use it for grocery and other retail items. So, they're really creating this kind of on demand commerce platform that really leverages their mobility footprint. So, um that is a very powerful flywheel when you compare to maybe um Instacart which is really focused on grocery does a little bit of food delivery. Um and similar to kind of door dash, which is really focused on meal delivery and increasingly grocery as well. So, they really have a lot of revenue streams tied to their platform and the subscription offering. So that's all, it's a lot of value there for the users.

01:13 Speaker A

In our robo taxi future, Nick, is Uber a winner or a victim?

01:22 Nick

We think it's a winner. We think it's a winner. This is one of the hottest debates when we talk to investors. Um ultimately, we believe selection is going to matter. What is really going to steer consumers? It's going to be pricing and convenience, or in other words, can I get a taxi service quickly? Or do I have to wait? So, ultimately, we think uh autonomous vehicles will be fragmented in the end. Selection and convenience are going to matter and Uber's got the most powerful distribution network.

01:46 Speaker A

I know you like Uber, Nick, got an outperform, right? So you're telling clients this one's a buy. What are the catalysts ahead, Nick, that you say, hey, it's going to keep moving this one higher?

01:58 Nick

I think we see a lot of partnership with Zeus, Nero, they have an Nvidia partnership. So as they start launching robot taxis across their platform this year, they're planning to get to 15 cities by the end of the year and many more after that. So once we get to see um these autonomous vehicles deployed on the platform and really get a a first hand look at the economics and the competitive landscape against Waymo and Tesla and other players. I think that will act as someone of a clearing event and help build confidence in kind of the trajectory Uber's developed so far are um year to day.

02:40 Speaker A

Let's talk about Instacart, Nick, because they reported. Investors not as excited about that one. What do you make of that print? What happened here?

02:51 Nick

Orders came in lighter than expected. Um so while they've delivered pretty strong revenue results and guidance was pretty good as well, the underlying kind of KPIs are how many how many orders are there and how much does each order cost? And orders came in lighter than expected, which suggests there may be some issues with uh uh the upper funnel and attracting more and more customers. And they even guided to that on the call that order growth um is likely to track with customer growth from here. And with third-party data, we see some stagnation in user growth. So I think investors are sniffing out while the kind of headline numbers look pretty good, some of the core inputs to durable growth uh may uh show some cracks right now, which is part of the reason we have an underperformed rating.

03:32 Speaker A

Customers are shifting to cheaper retailers. So I guess they're they're looking for value, they're looking for deals. How does that impact InstaCart in terms of, you know, take rate, profitability, Nick.

03:45 Nick

They probably divert consumers to platforms like Amazon, um potentially Walmart or other uh kind of more cost-effective channels. And people are often kind of weighing the deal versus the convenience and Amazon's the behemoth when it comes to cheap prices and very convenient experience because they can deliver, you know, same day next day for a large swath of kind of consumer staple type items.

title: Zuckerberg Just Put A Chunk of Meta's AI Bill On Wall Street's Credit Card
content:
Meta Platforms AI bill just got so large that one of Silicon Valley's richest companies went back to Wall Street for help.

On April 30, Meta sold $25 billion of senior unsecured bonds across six tranches. The deal came a day after the Mark Zuckerberg–led company raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast by $10 billion, to a new range of $125 billion to $145 billion. The capex hike, tied to AI infrastructure, rattled shareholders: Meta shares fell 9% the day after the announcement, in the biggest single-day slump since October.

That is what "Wall Street's credit card" means here. Zuckerberg did not personally borrow $25 billion, and Meta is not broke. This is not distress borrowing. It means the company is using the bond market to finance a large AI buildout rather than relying solely on its own cash flow.

The bond details show the scale and timeline for Meta to repay the borrowings. Meta's April 30 prospectus listed $3 billion of 4.55% notes due 2031, $2 billion of 4.875% notes due 2033, $6 billion of 5.25% notes due 2036, $4 billion of 6.2% notes due 2046, $6 billion of 6.3% notes due 2056 and $4 billion of 6.45% notes due 2066.

Net proceeds were estimated at about $24.9 billion, with the notes set to rank as unsecured senior obligations. The April sale was not a one-off. It followed Meta's $30 billion bond sale last year, its biggest ever.

The crucial nuance is that credit markets are not treating Meta like a weak borrower. S&P Global rated the new debt investment-grade and kept a stable outlook, but said Meta's massive AI investment was "starting to affect credit metrics."

That is the tension: Meta can afford the debt, but Zuckerberg's AI spending push is now large enough to matter to bond analysts.

Trending: Avoid the #1 Investing Mistake: How Your ‘Safe' Holdings Could Be Costing You Big Time

Independent market commentary has been sharper. Stephen Innes, writing in the investing blog The Dark Side Of The Boom, said "credit markets are starting to whisper what equities refuse to say out loud," pointing to Meta's CDS levels spiking to record highs as the company tapped the market for a "massive 25 billion bond issuance." He called it a sign of tension between "aggressive capex ambitions and deteriorating free cash flow."

The concern is not limited to Meta. Goldman Sachs said the AI spending boom has become enormous: "The scale of spending has increased considerably. Last quarter, consensus capital expenditure estimates for the largest cloud infrastructure companies jumped by $130 billion, reaching $670 billion for 2026. That's equivalent to more than 90% of their expected cash flows this year, according to our strategists."

Story Continues

So Zuckerberg did not max out a literal credit card. But Meta did put a meaningful chunk of its AI future onto Wall Street's balance sheet — and that makes the AI race a financing story, not just a technology story.

title: Tesla, Meta, Microsoft Investors May Need A 'Self-Destruct' Switch, Not Blind Faith
content:
Investors piling into the AI trade may need something less glamorous than another price target, product demo or promise about the future: a rule for when to stop trusting their favorite market narrative.

That is the central argument from the investing blog Capital Blueprint, helmed by an independent market commentator using the name Jin, who says investors should build what Jin calls a "self-destruct chip" into their AI framework — clear conditions that force them to stop trusting a favorite narrative when the evidence turns against it.

When A Thesis Hardens Into Doctrine

In Capital Blueprint's framing, the issue sits around "Microsoft,Google,Amazon, Meta,Tesla, and friends" — a group where the AI story has, the author writes, "hardened into something close to doctrine."

That does not mean AI is fake, or that the biggest AI-linked stocks are doomed. The point is sharper: a powerful investment thesis can become so familiar, so profitable and so emotionally comfortable that investors stop treating it as a thesis at all.

Don't Miss:

A single bad hire can set a startup back years. Here are the 5 hires founders most often misjudge — and why Still Learning the Market? These 50 Must-Know Terms Can Help You Catch Up Fast

They start treating it like an immutable truth.

That is where the "self-destruct" switch comes in. The phrase sounds dramatic, but the meaning is practical.

Investors should decide in advance what evidence would force them to rethink the AI trade — before a stock falls, before an earnings call disappoints and before the crowd finds a new explanation for why the story still works.

Jin frames the challenge bluntly: the key question is not only "How do I find the next great compounder?" It is also "How do I stop myself when I'm dangerously wrong?"

For AI investors, that discipline matters because many of these stocks are trading on long chains of future assumptions: autonomous driving, robotics, AI agents, cloud demand, advertising efficiency, enterprise productivity, data-center scale and years of expected profit growth.

Some of those assumptions may prove right. But the longer the forecast horizon, the easier it becomes for belief to outrun proof.

CapEx Is Cash Out The Door

Capital Blueprint also pushes back against one of the market's favorite shortcuts: the idea that massive AI capital spending automatically creates a moat.

Jin writes that "CapEx is cash out the door today." It may eventually return as durable, high-return cash flow — but that is the test, not the assumption.

Trending: Avoid the #1 Investing Mistake: How Your ‘Safe' Holdings Could Be Costing You Big Time

That is why Meta Platforms' latest spending plans matter.

Story Continues

The parent company of Facebook reported strong first-quarter results, including revenue of $56.31 billion, up 33% year over year, and free cash flow of $12.39 billion.

But it also raised its 2026 capex guidance to $125 billion to $145 billion, citing higher infrastructure costs, component pricing and data-center investment.

Strong business, bigger AI bill.

Different Companies, Same Test

Tesla Inc. faces a different version of the same discipline problem. Its story increasingly leans on autonomy, Robotaxi, robotics and AI infrastructure.

Those ambitions may prove valuable, but they still need tripwires: timelines, commercial proof, deployment milestones and evidence that the future is moving from promise to profit.

The same logic applies across Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com and other AI-linked leaders.

For cloud giants, the key test may be whether AI infrastructure spending converts into revenue growth, backlog, margins and customer stickiness.

For companies selling future autonomy or robotics, the test may be deployment, usage, unit economics and product timing.

For companies spending aggressively on data centers, the test may be whether the returns justify the cash leaving the business today.

See Also: Skip the Regrets: The Essential Retirement Tips Experts Wish Everyone Knew Earlier.

The broader market context makes Jin's point more urgent. Reuters reported that Goldman Sachs estimates terminal value — the value of corporate earnings beyond the next 10 years — accounts for about 75% of the S&P 500's equity value, near a 25-year high.

Goldman also estimated that a one-percentage-point drop in the assumed long-term growth rate could cut the S&P 500’s enterprise value by about 15%, with high-growth stocks hit harder.

That is the market-wide version of the "self-destruct" switch problem. When prices depend heavily on the distant future, small changes in belief can have huge consequences today.

When Conviction Crosses Into Belief

The switch is not a panic button. It is not a prediction that Tesla, Meta, Microsoft or the broader AI trade will fail.

It is a pre-agreed rule: if the facts move past this point, the thesis must be cut, reduced or rebuilt.

Without that kind of rule, every disappointment becomes patience. Every delay becomes vision. Every cost increase becomes investment. Every valuation stretch becomes "the market still doesn't get it."

That is how analysis turns into blind faith.

Capital Blueprint's argument does not ask investors to reject AI. It asks them to respect it enough to measure it. A real thesis should survive clear tests, while a fragile one needs vague promises.

The smartest AI investors may not be the ones with the loudest conviction. They may be the ones who know when conviction has crossed into belief — and when to flip the "self-destruct" switch.

title: Nio Inc (NIO) Goes After Tesla’s Lunch Again
content:
Nio Inc (NYSE:NIO) is one of the best large cap penny stocks under $10 to buy now. On April 28, Nio Inc (NYSE:NIO) launched its L80 model and immediately opened pre-orders for the car. The L80 is a two-row, 5-seat SUV that runs on battery power like all Nio cars. But the L80 is produced by Nio’s budget-focused sub-brand called Onvo.Nio Inc (NIO) Goes After Tesla’s Lunch Again

In terms of size, the L80 sits between the smaller L60 and the larger three-row L90 model. The L80 shares the platform and most components with the L90, but they differ in seating and cargo capacity.

The L80’s price starts at 245,800 yuan, making it cheaper than Tesla’s Model Y by 17,700 yuan in China. Model Y is the model to beat in the market segment that Nio is targeting with the L80.

The L80 deliveries are scheduled to begin on May 15. The earlier Onvo model launches had a strong debut. For instance, the flagship L60 surpassed 20,000 unit deliveries in the first 100 days. The L90 exceeded 10,000 unit deliveries in the first month.

Nio is expanding its budget model lineup as it also pushes to improve profitability. The company posted its first-ever adjusted operating profit in Q4 2025. Looking ahead, Nio plans to reduce costs and lift its bottom line by producing its own chips. The company’s CEO, William ‌Li, shared this plan in an interview with Reuters on April 24.

Nio Inc (NYSE:NIO) is a Chinese automaker that produces electric cars. Its portfolio includes a variety of sedans and SUVs. In addition to cars, Nio also makes smartphones and other tech products. The company was founded in 2014 and is headquartered in Shanghai.

title: Insider Alert: Tesla Director Offloads Nearly $10 Million in Stock
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) board director Kathleen Wilson-Thompson sold about $9.98 million worth of shares on April 30 through multiple transactions conducted under a pre-set trading arrangement.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) The transactions were tied to previously exercised options and executed at varying prices, the filing showed.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) said the director exercised 40,948 stock options granted at $14.99 each before selling 27,389 shares in a series of staged transactions. The options had fully vested in 2022, allowing conversion into common equity, according to the disclosure.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) transactions were carried out under a Rule 10b5-1 plan established in November 2025, a framework designed to schedule insider sales in advance and reduce timing discretion. Following the activity, the director retained about 48,399 shares, the filing indicated.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) filings showed the move aligned with standard board compensation practices tied to long-term equity awards. The disclosure did not include operational updates or changes to company guidance, and the activity was framed within routine governance-related portfolio adjustments.
